pdf_filename: Gamification, Pandemic and Learning the History of Ideas. Experiments in the Context of Core Curriculum.pdf

bibliographic.title: Gamification, Pandemic and Learning the History of Ideas. Experiments in the Context of Core Curriculum
bibliographic.venue: RIED-Revista Iberoamericana de Educación a Distancia

study_characteristics.sample_description: 23 students across four courses of the Core Curriculum subject 'Contemporary Civilization' (a history of Western philosophy from Plato to Freud) at Universidad Adolfo Ibáñez in Chile. First-year students from law, psychology, journalism, commercial engineering, and civil engineering programs.
study_characteristics.study_design: Qualitative autoethnographic research (teacher-researcher autoethnography with ethnographic recording of student interventions)
study_characteristics.game_type: Serious games (custom-designed tabletop/role-playing games conducted via Zoom)
study_characteristics.game_name: Multiple serious games: El Juego de Giges, El Juego de la Caverna, El Juego del Concilio, El Juego de Urticario Crudelis, El Juego del Colono, El Juego de los Sueños, El Juego del Contrato, El Juego del Manifiesto, El Juego de los Espectros, Decisión Final
study_characteristics.aim: To examine the rationale and results of a gamification experiment based on serious games in the context of teaching the history of ideas (Western philosophy from Plato to Freud) during the COVID-19 pandemic, investigating how games develop essential skills for critical comprehension of the history of ideas including hermeneutic and intersubjective reasoning, historical imagination, sense of contingency, and contextualization ability.

eligibility.concerns: The study focuses on the history of ideas/philosophy rather than history in the strict disciplinary sense, though it is framed within humanities education and involves historical thinking skills. The study is qualitative with no control group or quantitative measures.

rq1.conceptualization: The authors conceptualize gamification through the lens of serious games drawing on classical play theory. They reference Huizinga (2005), Bally (1973), and Fink (2016) to understand games as creating fictional worlds based on imagination with internal logical coherence and aesthetic harmony. Games involve the creation of a para-identity where the player assumes a role distinct from ordinary social identities, engaging in a self-conscious fictional activity. The game is characterized as essentially a ritual — a dramatized action socializing a universe of symbols and norms — that creates a bounded playground space and a suspension of ordinary chronological time. The authors use the term 'serious games' (juegos serios) following López Raventós (2016), distinguishing their approach from mere gamification elements, and emphasize the cognitive and epistemological powers of play.
theoretical_frameworks: Bally's theory of play as expression of freedom
Fink's philosophy of play as symbol of the world
Hermeneutic tradition (fusion of horizons, historical consciousness)
Seixas (2017) on historical consciousness and historical thinking
Froeyman (2016) on ethical turn in historiography
Autoethnographic methodology (Adams, Ellis, Holman Jones, Bochner)

rq2.key_outcomes: The study reports qualitative outcomes from autoethnographic field notes across 10 serious games played over 80 sessions. Key findings include: (1) Games developed 'historical consciousness' — the ability to reflect critically on historical time and understand the otherness of past societies. (2) Students developed hermeneutic and intersubjective reasoning by establishing conceptual mediations with historical characters. (3) Games fostered historical imagination — the ability to construct abstract concepts and fictional scenarios from diverse experiences. (4) Students developed a sense of contingency — understanding that philosophical ideas are not universal truths but mental constructions within specific spatiotemporal coordinates. (5) Games promoted contextualization ability — students learned to situate authors' thought in precise spatiotemporal coordinates. (6) The fictional para-identity of gameplay created a 'radical otherness' that allowed students to think beyond their usual values and worldviews. (7) Games served as epistemic rituals breaking pandemic monotony and the productivist time of virtual education. (8) Group identifications formed during games translated into real friendships, overcoming pandemic isolation.
rq2.engagement_results: Students became highly engaged with the game activities. In the Juego de los Sueños, after the first session students spontaneously requested a winner be declared and asked for explanations about which team's solution best reflected Descartes' philosophy, showing that victory and quality of reflection mattered equally. Students broke the solipsism of the pandemic through game-based group identification. The games functioned as 'pure events' that disrupted the cadence of quarantines and virtual deliveries, adding narrativity to the courses.

game_design_elements: Decision-making by groups (toma de decisiones por grupos)
Team debate (juego de equipos de debate)
Imagination and guessing games with uchronic thinking (juego de imaginación y adivinanza; pensamiento ucrónico)
Vital decisions by teams (juego de decisiones vitales por equipos)
Fictional scenarios connected to contemporary issues
technological_platforms: Zoom (video conferencing platform for all sessions)
instructional_strategies: Pre-assigned readings from philosophical canon texts (one book every week and a half)
Three participatory sessions per book with professor as coordinator
Connection of philosophical texts to contemporary everyday dilemmas and current affairs in Chile, Latin America, and the world
Hermeneutic strategies for game development in class
Recording of spoken interventions (sounds) and written interventions (chats/texts) in each session
Final game (Decisión Final) as summative assessment comparing all 21 philosophers studied
rq3.content_integration: Each serious game was directly tied to specific philosophical texts from the syllabus covering Western philosophy from Plato to Freud. Games required students to apply the ideas from the assigned readings to fictional scenarios that connected historical philosophical concepts to contemporary issues. For example, El Juego de Giges required applying Plato's concept of justice to a modern dilemma about Ukrainian refugees; El Juego de la Caverna used Plato and Aristotle's theories to reorganize society in a post-apocalyptic future; El Juego del Contrato placed students as French Revolution characters negotiating a constitution based on Rousseau's Social Contract. The content integration was deep — game evaluation criteria assessed mastery of the philosophical texts and the ability to apply historical ideas to present-day contexts.

implementation_barriers: COVID-19 pandemic forced all sessions online via Zoom, creating distance that disincentivized student intervention and interest
Virtualization of teaching posed challenges for highly participatory Core Curriculum sessions
Students' faces were rarely visible during Zoom sessions (cameras off), making interaction more difficult
The pandemic eliminated physical meeting spaces, created a destabilized sense of time, and increased neoliberal academic productivism pressures
Humanities teaching was particularly harmed by the pandemic context
methodology_limitations: Autoethnographic method limits findings to the teacher-researcher's professional experience perspective
No quantitative data or control group — findings are purely qualitative
Limitations are tied to the pedagogical-didactic interest of the research, as objectives included provoking new teaching-learning formats
Results are based on field diary notes and recordings, subject to researcher interpretation
Small sample size (23 students across 4 course sections)
negative_effects: In El Juego del Contrato, many teams could not reach agreements when reconciling their characters' particular objectives with a general will, discarding solutions from Rousseauian theory of popular sovereignty
Some students were implicitly confronted with choosing between uncomfortable complex truths and comfortable self-serving virtual reality of social media 'likes' and safe spaces
mitigation_strategies: Gamification was adopted specifically as a response to the challenges of virtualized teaching during the pandemic
Games were designed to create engagement and break the monotony of pandemic distance learning
The serious game format created ritual-like 'pure events' that disrupted the alienating cadence of quarantine
Group-based gameplay fostered social connections that helped overcome pandemic isolation
Authors argue the approach should be systematized for use in post-pandemic contexts as well

domain1.q1_evidence: The study focuses on a specific, well-defined context: four courses of Contemporary Civilization at Universidad Adolfo Ibáñez, Chile, with 23 students over 80 sessions from March 2020 to December 2021. The selection is clearly defined by the institutional context.
domain1.q2_evidence: The sample of 23 students is from a single university in Chile, taking a specific Core Curriculum course. There is no discussion of how representative this sample is of broader student populations. The unique pandemic context and the specific institutional setting (Core Curriculum model adopted from Columbia University) limits generalizability.

domain2.q3_evidence: Data collection relies entirely on autoethnographic field notes and ethnographic recordings (spoken and written student interventions). While the authors reference established autoethnographic methodologies (Adams, Ellis, Holman Jones, Bochner), no validated instruments or standardized assessment tools were used. The evaluation of game outcomes is based on the teacher-researcher's subjective interpretation of field diary notes.
domain2.q4_evidence: Analysis is qualitative, based on the construction of a chronological narrative from field notes organized around four objectives. There is no systematic coding methodology described, no inter-rater reliability, and no triangulation with other data sources beyond the teacher-researcher's perspective. The authors acknowledge their limitations are tied to the autoethnographic approach.

domain3.q5_evidence: The findings are consistently interpreted within the theoretical framework of play theory (Huizinga, Bally, Fink) and hermeneutic tradition. The authors present rich qualitative descriptions of each game's outcomes. However, the interpretation is uniformly positive with limited critical examination of potential negative outcomes or failures.
domain3.q6_evidence: The authors briefly acknowledge limitations of the autoethnographic method (findings tied to teacher-researcher perspective, pedagogical-didactic interest). However, the discussion of limitations is relatively thin — there is no discussion of confirmation bias, observer effect, or the inherent limitations of the teacher evaluating their own pedagogical intervention.

risk_of_bias.overall_justification: The study presents a rich qualitative autoethnographic account of gamification in history of ideas education during the pandemic. However, several factors contribute to high risk of bias: (1) the teacher-researcher is both the designer/implementer of the games and the sole evaluator of outcomes, with no independent assessment; (2) no validated measurement instruments were used; (3) analysis lacks systematic methodology (no coding scheme, no inter-rater reliability); (4) findings are uniformly positive with minimal critical self-examination; (5) small, non-representative sample from a single institution; (6) no comparison group or pre-post measures. While the autoethnographic approach is methodologically legitimate, the lack of triangulation and the dual role of the researcher as both participant and evaluator create substantial risk of bias.
